intro: Degsne maps three trees across Prienai district: a larch standing 49 metres tall in a stand planted in 1849, the tallest tree recorded anywhere in Lithuania, the Budininkai Oak, 31 metres tall and one of 47 oaks given nature-monument status in June 2026, 6.4 kilometres away in the same forestry district, and the Bagrenas Linden, a forked, hollowing lime on a village street 12 to 17 kilometres further out. Published thin because the tallest tree is destination enough on its own, not because Degsne's research is finished.
meta_description: The Degsne Forest Larch, Lithuania's tallest recorded tree at 49 metres, with the nearby Budininkai Oak and the Bagrenas village linden.
question_meta: Degsne's tallest tree is a 49-metre larch, the tallest recorded in Lithuania, with a protected oak and a village linden nearby.
question_answer: Degsne's mapped trees are the Degsne Forest Larch, a European larch 49 metres tall in the Degsne forest stand of Nemuno Loops Regional Park, the tallest tree recorded in Lithuania, the Budininkai Oak, 31 metres tall, 6.4 kilometres away in the same state forest complex, and the Bagrenas Linden, a forked village lime 12 to 17 kilometres further out.
question_context: The tallest tree in Lithuania is a larch, and it is under two metres round. At 49 metres it beats everything else growing in the country, and the State Protected Areas Service register lists it under exactly that title. The trunk carries no green branch at all for its first 29 metres, and at chest height it measures 186 centimetres round, a demonstration of how a larch puts its growth upward rather than outward. The first larches here were planted in 1849, and the stand they grew into is now the tallest forest in Lithuania, averaging around 42 metres. The forest was protected in 1960, and this one tree was designated in its own right in 2002. No legend attaches to it beyond the record itself. Getting there takes a car or a bicycle: a gravel forest road runs about three kilometres off the Kaunas to Alytus road north of Balbieriskis, and no bus goes near it. Six kilometres away in the same forestry district stands the Budininkai Oak, 31 metres tall, one of 47 oaks a single June 2026 order gave nature-monument status at once; not a walk from the larch, but a plausible pairing for anyone driving out.

faq.q: What is the tallest tree in Degsne?
faq.a: The Degsne Forest Larch, 49 metres tall, the tallest tree recorded anywhere in Lithuania.
The larches here were planted in 1849, making the stand around 175 years old, a documented planting date for the forest rather than an estimate.

faq.q: Why is the trunk so thin for such a tall tree?
faq.a: Larches put most of their growth upward rather than outward. At 186 centimetres round it is slender for its height, and the trunk carries no branch at all for its first 29 metres.

Yes, it stands in public state forest within Nemuno Loops Regional Park, reached by a gravel forest road with no gate or permission needed. There is no public transport to the road itself; a car or bicycle is the practical way in.

faq.q: Is there a third tree here?
faq.a: Yes, the Bagrenas Linden, a forked and hollowing lime on the main street of Bagrenas village, 12 to 17 kilometres from the larch and the oak. It is a separate car stop rather than a walk from either.

trees.name: The Degsnė Forest Larch

location.address: Degsnė Forest, Balbieriškis forestry district, Nemuno Loops Regional Park, Prienai District, Lithuania; via a gravel forest road off the Kaunas-Alytus road (route 130), about 3km north of Balbieriškis / 7km south of Prienai
location.neighbourhood: Degsnė Forest, Nemuno Loops Regional Park

trees.access: Free, public state forest within Nemuno Loops Regional Park. Reached by a good-quality gravel forest road, about 2.5-3km off route 130 (Kaunas-Alytus), turning off shortly before the Balbieriškis outcrop (Balbieriškio atodanga). No gate or permission needed.
trees.transport: No public transport reaches the forest road itself; nearest towns are Balbieriškis (about 3km) and Prienai (about 7km). A car or bicycle is the practical way in.
trees.story:
The tallest tree in Lithuania is a larch, and it is under two metres round.

At 49 metres it beats everything else growing in the country, and the State Protected Areas Service register lists it under exactly that title. It is a demonstration of what larches do with their energy: nearly all of it goes upward. The trunk carries no green branch at all for its first 29 metres, and at chest height it measures 186 centimetres round. Anyone arriving with a churchyard oak in mind is looking for the wrong shape entirely.

It did not turn up by accident. The first larches here were planted in 1849, when this was a corner of the Russian Empire, and the stand they grew into is now the tallest forest in Lithuania, averaging around 42 metres. The forest was protected in 1960. This one tree was designated in its own right in 2002, by which point it had stood through two world wars and watched Lithuania become an independent country twice. A survey that year called its condition satisfactory, with the first signs of age on it.

No legend attaches to it, which feels right. The record is the story.

Getting there takes a car or a bicycle. A gravel forest road runs about three kilometres off the Kaunas to Alytus road north of Balbieriškis, and no bus goes near it.

best_time.label: late October, when the larch turns gold and drops its needles

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest tree around by far, 49m up on a trunk under two metres round, bare of branches for its first 29 metres. It stands off a gravel forest road in Degsne Forest, Nemuno Loops park.

trees.name: Būdininkai Oak

location.address: Būdininkai village, Prienai district, Lithuania, in Balbieriškis Forest, about 1.7km south of the A16 (Vilnius-Prienai-Marijampolė) highway, reached via a gravel road from the Naujosios Ūtos bus stop
location.neighbourhood: Būdininkai village, Balbieriškis Forest, Prienai district

trees.access: Free, public. Stands in Balbieriškis Forest, a 2,855-hectare state-important forest (Prienai Forest Management Board's Naujoji Ūta / Degsnė forestry districts), the same forest complex the already-published Degsnė Forest Larch stands in. Reached via a gravel road off the A16 highway at the Naujosios Ūtos bus stop, toward the Balbieriškis forest biosphere-polygon boundary marker. No gate, fee or private land involved.
trees.transport: No public transport reaches the tree itself; nearest stop is Naujoji Ūta on the A16 (Vilnius-Prienai-Marijampolė), then a gravel forest road on foot, bike or by car. About 6.4km from the Degsnė Forest Larch (deg_001), a plausible day-trip pairing within the same forest, though not a walk between the two.
trees.story:
The order that made this oak a protected national monument is dated June 2026, which makes it one of the newest protected trees in Lithuania and one of the least written about. It arrived on the list with 30 other oaks, a run of limes and six boulders. The same order draws a protection zone around the trunk: 0.041 hectares, roughly 410 square metres of forest floor that now belongs to the tree.

It is 31 metres tall and 4.85 metres round at chest height, standing in Balbieriškis Forest, 2,855 hectares of state forest in the Prienai district. Walk around it and it changes character. One side is in good order and carries heavy branches; the other is lichened over with damaged bark. That is what a large oak in a working forest actually looks like up close, and it is more worth the walk than a postcard specimen.

It has an official sibling. Būdininkų II was protected under the same order and stands nearby, which is how a forest ends up with numbered trees. Lithuania's tallest tree, a larch, grows 6.4 kilometres away in the same forestry district, close enough to make an afternoon of the two, though not close enough to walk between them.

Nobody has published an age for this oak. If you have seen a figure on a sign or in a survey, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its lopsided condition, one side healthy with heavy branches, the other lichened over with damaged bark. It stands in Balbieriskis Forest near Budininkai village.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: Bagrėnas Linden

location.address: Liepų g. 132, Bagrėnas village, Prienai district

trees.access: Free; stands beside the main street of Bagrėnas village, near an old homestead at Liepų g. 132. No source states whether the roadside spot itself is fenced; treat it as visible and reachable from the public village street, the same honest caveat already used for other homestead-adjacent trees in this district (compare Kaunas kun_006).
trees.transport: No public transport; reached by car via road KK130, then about 3.4km southeast into Bagrėnas village. Roughly 12-17km by straight-line distance from Degsnė's other two trees (deg_001, deg_002) in Balbieriškis Forest; real road distance is likely greater. A plausible day-trip pairing in the same district, not a walk between the two.
trees.story:
Measure this lime at chest height and you get 5.45 metres of single trunk. Half a metre higher it stops being one tree: the stem forks in two, and the base underneath it is hollowed and split open.

Lithuania made it a state-protected natural heritage object in March 2026 and drew a protection zone of 0.028 hectares around it, roughly 280 square metres of village ground that now belongs to the tree. The designation is that recent, which is also why almost nothing has been written about the tree. Beyond its register entry and a single Lithuanian reference page, it has gone undescribed.

What stands there is 27.5 metres of lime on the main street of Bagrėnas, beside an old homestead, at an address that reads Liepų gatvė 132. Linden Street.

Nobody has published an age. A girth on its own will not honestly produce one either, not for a lime: they fork, hollow out and put on wood at rates too variable for the arithmetic to mean much. If somebody has dated this one, tell us and the figure goes on the page.

Getting there means a car. Degsnė's other two trees stand 12 to 17 kilometres off in Balbieriškis Forest, which makes an unhurried afternoon of all three and is far more than anyone is walking between them.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting in two about 1.8 metres up, above a base that is hollowed and split open, 5.45 metres round below the fork. It stands on the main street of Bagrėnas, beside the homestead at Liepų g. 132.

best_time.label: June to July, when the lime flowers and the whole street smells of it
